disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, impulsivity, and difficulty inhibiting actions, with relatively fewer prominent inattentive symptoms. Adults may present with chronic inner restlessness, difficulty staying seated, excessive talking, and interrupting others, often leading to occupational, relational, or legal problems. Symptoms typically begin in childhood, but in some individuals they become clinically significant or are first recognized later in life when environmental demands change or compensatory strategies fail. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, and personality disorders by its early onset, pervasive pattern across settings, and specific profile of hyperactive-impulsive behaviors rather than episodic or situational agitation.

narrative.stressor: Over the past year, Nilda shifted from mostly solo surveillance work to a contract with a large law firm that requires her to spend long hours in conference rooms reviewing files and sitting through structured case conferences. For the first time in her career, she has to remain in one place for extended periods, follow rigid meeting agendas, and sit quietly while senior partners talk through strategy, which clashes with the more mobile, self‑paced style she has always relied on. Over the last eight months, her difficulty tolerating these new demands has started to interfere with her reputation for calm professionalism, drawing comments from colleagues about her restlessness and making her worry that she will lose this lucrative contract. After an uncomfortable incident where a partner pulled her aside to ask if she was "bored or anxious" during a key meeting, she became concerned enough about how out of control her behavior felt compared to her disciplined self‑image that she agreed, at the urging of a younger mentee who has ADHD, to seek a psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: “In these long client and attorney meetings, I just can’t stay in my seat—I keep having to get up and move around even when I know it looks unprofessional.”

narrative.stressor: Marco’s district recently promoted him into a part‑time instructional coach role on top of his classroom duties, which means long committee meetings, formal presentations, and supervising other teachers instead of the more free‑flowing, music‑filled classroom environment he thrives in. As these responsibilities ramped up over the last eight months, his difficulty containing his energy and his habit of jumping into conversations began to strain relationships with colleagues, who started complaining that he dominated discussions and derailed agendas. The combination of complaints from younger teachers, formal feedback from his principal about his conduct in meetings, and his wife’s observation that he seemed "always wound up and talking over everyone" left him worried that his position and reputation were at risk. When his principal gently suggested that what they were seeing might be more than just enthusiasm and recommended he talk to a professional, Marco finally agreed to an evaluation after years of brushing off similar concerns.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I keep cutting people off and jumping into their conversations at work, even when I tell myself to stop—I feel like I’m constantly intruding on others.”

narrative.stressor: In the last year, Idalmis began transitioning toward partial retirement, giving up some of her teaching load and administrative duties with the expectation that life would finally slow down. Instead, with fewer structured professional demands, she filled her time with community events, cultural workshops, gardening projects, and frequent visits with grandchildren, unintentionally creating long, unstructured days at home and in the community. Over the past eight months, she has become increasingly aware that when she is not anchored by the tight bell schedules and meeting agendas of school, her lifelong tendency to be constantly in motion has become more pronounced, to the point that her husband and close friends have commented that she can’t seem to sit and relax through a simple book club meeting or family dinner. Concerned that this restlessness might be a sign of anxiety or another late‑life problem, and prompted by a colleague who recently received an adult ADHD diagnosis, she sought a psychiatric consultation to understand why slowing down has felt so uncomfortable and difficult.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Now that I’m supposed to be slowing down, I feel like I’m always on the go and can’t just sit still and relax, even for a short visit or a quiet meal.”
